lines.text: Q
3.4 Cooking, Roughage and Water
Have you noticed that a raw carrot snaps and a boiled one bends? That spinach
loses its bright green in the pan?
Heat changes food, and not only in ways we can see. Some nutrients — Vitamin C
among them — are partly destroyed by high heat. Washing vegetables and fruit
after cutting or peeling them washes some vitamins away as well.
Two sensible conclusions follow. First, include some fruit and raw vegetables in your
diet so that not everything you eat has been through a hot pan. Second, wash
produce before you cut it, not after.
But do wash it. Thoroughly, every time. The vitamins lost to washing are a small
price against the dirt, pesticide residue and germs that washing removes.
Ira: So every nutrient we need
comes from a plant or an animal?
Aarav: ThatG what
the chapter says.
A„seawater. Or rock.
Ira: Then where does salt
come from? Not a plant.
Not an animal.
Ira: And Vitamin D — the
teacher said our own skin
makes it in sunlight. That
isn't food either.
Ira is right on both counts, and there are two more things the body needs that
are not nutrients at all.
Roughage, also called dietary fibre, comes mainly from plant foods — whole
grains, pulses, fruit with its skin, green leafy vegetables, nuts. Roughage supplies
no nutrients whatsoever. The body cannot digest it. That is precisely the point:
it gives the digestive system bulk to work against, moving waste through and out.
Without enough of it, the gut slows and constipation follows.
Water supplies no nutrients either, and nothing works without it. Water carries
nutrients from the gut into the blood, carries waste out through sweat and urine,
and holds the body's temperature steady. Drink it regularly through the day rather
than in one gulp when you are already thirsty.
THINK-SPOT
Which foods give you water besides water itself? List four.
